chunks: With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
In the book of ʿAlī عليه السلام: “Indeed, the cat is a beast, and there is no harm in its leftover drink, and I am ashamed before Allah to leave food because the cat has eaten from it.”

Al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: There is no harm in performing wudu (ablution) from the leftover water of horses, mules, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and that from which the rest of the birds have drunk, except those among them that eat carrion; for wudu (ablution) with the leftover of what they have drunk from is disliked. And if it drank from it while there was on its beak a trace of blood and the like, it is not to be used in taharah (ritual purification) in any case.

This is indicated by the report that we have cited from Ḥarīz from Abī al-ʿAbbās al-Faḍl; and this is also indicated by what we have narrated from Samāʿah from Abī Baṣīr from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام; and this also indicates it.

key_terms.الْجِيَفَ: carrion, dead carcasses eaten by scavenging birds
key_terms.سُؤْرِهِ: its leftover drink or remnant after drinking
key_terms.فَضْلَةِ: leftover water remaining after an animal has drunk from it

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to use water or eat food after a cat or other animals have drunk from or eaten from it?
ai.summary: This passage addresses rulings of taharah (ritual purity) concerning the leftover water or food touched by animals. It states that a cat’s leftover is unobjectionable, and discusses the permissibility or dislike of using water drunk from by various animals and birds, especially carrion-eating birds or those whose beaks bear traces of blood.
